title: Trait Objects (dyn)
intro: A trait object is a value whose exact type is forgotten, and only the trait's methods remain. It is how one list holds squares and rectangles, or one variable holds "whichever shape we picked at run time". You write `dyn Shape`, and you hold it behind a pointer.

coming_from.go: `&dyn Shape` and `Box<dyn Shape>` are interface values: a pointer to the data plus a pointer to a table of methods. `Vec<Box<dyn Shape>>` is your `[]Shape`. The differences: a type must say `impl Shape for Square` first, a `&dyn Shape` points at the original where a Go interface copies the value, and in Rust you choose per use between this and a generic `<T: Shape>`, which is decided at compile time.
coming_from.kotlin: A `Box<dyn Shape>` is a `Shape` reference: the object sits on the heap and each call finds the right method at run time. In Kotlin every call through an interface works like that. In Rust it is something you ask for with `dyn`. A Kotlin `<T : Shape>` is erased and still an interface call; Rust's `<T: Shape>` is compiled once per type, with a direct call.
coming_from.python: Python needs nothing like this to hold a mix: any object with an `area()` method goes in a list, and the method is found by name when the call runs. In Rust the list is `Vec<Box<dyn Shape>>`, each type must say `impl Shape` first, and a type without it is refused at compile time, not when the call runs.
coming_from.typescript: `Shape[]` is `Vec<Box<dyn Shape>>`. TypeScript checks shape (any object with an `area()` counts) and the interface is erased at run time. In Rust a type must say `impl Shape for Square`, and a `dyn Shape` carries its method table with it.
coming_from.java: `List<Shape>` is `Vec<Box<dyn Shape>>`. In Java every object sits behind a reference and an interface call picks the method by the object's class at run time. Rust asks you to write both parts, `Box` and `dyn`. A Java `<T extends Shape>` is erased and still an interface call; Rust's `<T: Shape>` is compiled once per type, with a direct call.
coming_from.csharp: `List<IShape>` is `Vec<Box<dyn Shape>>`. A class instance is always behind a reference in C# and an interface call picks the method by the object's type at run time. Rust asks you to write both parts, `Box` and `dyn`. Its generic `<T: Shape>` is closest to a C# generic with a struct type argument, and a struct behind an interface is boxed, as a `Square` is in a `Box<dyn Shape>`.
coming_from.c: `main.c` builds a `dyn` by hand: a struct holding a data pointer and a pointer to a table of function pointers. A `&dyn Shape` is the same idea, filled in and checked by the compiler, with drop, size and alignment added to the table.
coming_from.cpp: `Box<dyn Shape>` is a `std::unique_ptr<Shape>` calling `virtual` methods, with one difference in layout: the pointer to the table sits in the pointer, not inside every object, so `Square` stays a plain struct and only a `dyn` pays for the table.

notes: `dyn Shape` means "some type that implements `Shape`, known only at run time". Its size is not known, so you cannot hold one by value. You hold it behind a pointer: `&dyn Shape`, `&mut dyn Shape`, or `Box<dyn Shape>`. A `Box` is an owned pointer to a value on the heap.
A `Vec` holds values of one type and one size. `Box<dyn Shape>` is one type and one size whatever it contains, so a `Vec<Box<dyn Shape>>` can hold squares and rectangles side by side.

The call `s.area()` looks up the right `area` through a table at run time. That is dynamic dispatch. The compile-time alternative is a generic `fn f<T: Shape>(s: &T)`, which the compiler writes once per type.

Only some traits can be used as `dyn`, because the compiler must be able to build the table. A method with its own type parameter, or one that returns `Self`, makes the trait unusable as `dyn` unless that method says `where Self: Sized`.

gotcha.title: A list of a trait, without Box<dyn>
gotcha.looks_fine: In Go, Kotlin, Java, C# and TypeScript, a list whose element type is an interface holds any mix of implementing types.
gotcha.rust_sees: `Shape` is a trait, not a type. It names a whole set of types of different sizes, and a `Vec` needs every element to be the same size. The compiler asks for `dyn`, and after that it asks for a pointer.
gotcha.why: Those languages give the list an element of one fixed size: a reference (Kotlin, Java, C#, TypeScript) or, in Go, a two-word interface value that holds a copy of the value and points at it. Rust stores values where you put them and does not add a pointer on its own, so you write the pointer: `Box<dyn Shape>`.

go.says: Go runs this and prints total: 33. An interface value is always the same size (two words) and holds a copy of the value, so `[]Shape` holds a mix.

kotlin.says: Kotlin runs this and prints total: 33. A `List<Shape>` holds references, which are all the same size.

python.says: Python prints total: 33. A list holds references to objects, and there is no declared element type to satisfy.

typescript.says: Prints total: 33. A `Shape[]` holds references to objects of any class that fits the interface.

java.says: Java runs this and prints total: 33. A `List<Shape>` holds references, so it holds any mix of implementing classes.

csharp.says: C# runs this and prints total: 33. A `List<IShape>` holds references to class instances.

c.says: C has no traits. A mixed array is an array of structs holding a data pointer and a function table, as `main.c` shows.

cpp.says: C++ refuses this too: an array (or a `std::vector`) of `Shape` stores `Shape` objects themselves, and `Shape` is abstract. The usual fix is the same as in Rust, pointers: `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Shape>>`.
